title: Serving Economics Decision Guide: Balancing Cost, Latency, and Fidelity
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

Summary
This decision guide helps product managers, solution engineers, and sales engineers choose and justify serving configurations for customer workloads. It codifies tradeoffs between cost (per-token or per-embedding unit), latency SLOs, and output fidelity. The guidance covers hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes and includes a structured decision flow, concrete cost examples, fidelity tier mapping, rollout checklist, and telemetry requirements.

Intended audience
- Product managers and pricing leads
- Solutions and sales engineers supporting customer sizing and contracts
- SRE/Platform engineers advising on deployment choices
- Customer success and technical account managers (TAMs)

When to use this doc
- During presales sizing and pricing conversations
- When proposing migration from hosted to Dedicated or Private
- When customers request cost vs. quality tradeoff trade studies

Context and constraints
- Applies to Redwood Inference serving surface as of 2029-02.
- Assumes access to the current model catalog and quantization profiles.
- Not a substitute for per-customer benchmarking. Run a short finalist benchmark when fidelity is critical.

Decision framework (short)
1) Classify the workload by business impact and latency sensitivity: Critical (user-facing synchronous, sub-200ms), Important (interactive, 200–800ms), Batch/Analytics (>800ms).
2) Map to fidelity tier: High (human-comparative), Medium (task-competent), Low (best-effort/semantic).
3) Choose deployment mode: Hosted for low-friction and discovery, Dedicated for 24/7 throughput predictability or data isolation, Private for compliance or network-local latency.
4) Configure economic levers: batching, KV-prefix caching, quantization profile, fallback model set, and per-route SLO creditization.
5) Validate via a 3-day representative traffic replay (see appendix: benchmark checklist).

Workload classification details
- Latency SLO examples:
  - Sub-100ms: conversational telephony, real-time recommendation.
  - 100–300ms: chat or autocomplete in editor.
  - 300–800ms: interactive analytics or summarization.
  - >800ms: offline batch embedding/semantic similarity jobs.
- Fidelity examples:
  - High fidelity: multi-turn dialog with brand voice, legal summarization, hallucination-sensitive content.
  - Medium fidelity: search re-ranking, customer support assistants with canned fallbacks.
  - Low fidelity: exploratory research, embedding generation for indexing.

Deployment guidance
Hosted (default)
- Strengths: fastest time-to-value, automatic model catalog updates, predictable per-unit billing for most customers.
- Recommended when: workload is non-sensitive, traffic is bursty or exploratory, and peak latency targets are moderate (>=200ms).
- Economic levers: enable request-level caching, client-side batching, light quantization (e.g., 8-bit).
- Limitations: noisy neighbor risk for extremely high sustained throughput; fallback ramping may be slower under contention.

Dedicated
- Strengths: reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput, isolated performance.
- Recommended when: sustained high throughput, low jitter requirements, or enterprise customers demanding SLA-backed latency/availability.
- Economic levers: dedicated autoscaling policies, controlled batch windows, larger quantization experiments allowed.
- Pricing note: includes reserved monthly commitment; use the capacity-sim calculator (see appendix) to convert expected QPS and average sequence length into a commitment.

Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Strengths: full network proximity, compliance, and data residency.
- Recommended when: regulated workloads, air-gapped requirements, or customers with strict outbound networking policies.
- Economic levers: hardware selection, local caching layers, and close control of model variants.
- Sales guidance: price as an enterprise engagement (platform + support); include hardware amortization and on-prem maintenance in proposals.

Fidelity tiers and model choices
- Fidelity tier -> model and quantization guidance:
  - High: use base LLM variants with FP16 or 4-bit float (Q4F16) profiles; do not quantize aggressively. Use largest compatible model family listed in the model catalog.
  - Medium: accept 8-bit/4-bit integer quantization (Q8_INT / Q4_INT) with small prompt engineering to preserve style. Consider using a medium-size variant (e.g., medium-1) and enable prefix caching.
  - Low: aggressive quantization (Q4_INT8 or lower) or distilled models. Favor throughput-optimized kernels and best-effort fallbacks.

Tradeoff matrix (example)
| Requirement        | Hosted recommended | Dedicated recommended | Private recommended | Notes |
|--------------------|--------------------|-----------------------|----------------------|-------|
| Sub-200ms SLO      | Limited (burst)    | Yes                   | Yes                  | Dedicated preferred for <150ms stable SLOs |
| 24/7 high QPS       | No                 | Yes                   | Optional             | Use Dedicated commits |
| Compliance (SOC2/PCI)| Possible with hosted controls | Yes          | Yes                  | Private for strict data residency |
| Lowest unit cost    | For small, bursty usage | For sustained high throughput | Depends on amortized infra |

Economic levers explained
- Batching: Larger batches reduce per-token latency amortization but increase tail latency. Set per-route max_batch_size and max_wait_ms based on SLO.
- KV prefix caching: High benefit for chat-heavy, repeated context. Recommend cache hit target >= 30% for conversation apps.
- Quantization profile: Use the quality-aware quantization rollout PRD for A/B testing across fidelity lanes.
- Model fallback set: Define a single-step fallback (High->Medium) and a two-step set (High->Medium->Low) for extreme congestion. Include fidelity-preserving prompts for fallback.

Rollout checklist (for customers moving from Hosted -> Dedicated/Private)
1) Pre-sales sizing: collect representative traces, 7-day traffic histogram of QPS, 50/95/99 latency targets, and average tokens per request.
2) Benchmark: run 3-day synthetic and replay tests at 1.25x expected peak QPS. Capture latency percentiles, token cost, kernel utilization.
3) Cost model: estimate committed capacity (GPUs), monthly amortized infra, per-token costs, and margin. Use the capacity-sim calculator.
4) Configuration playbook: set routing policy, model pinning, cache config, and autoscaling bounds.
5) SLO and monitoring: create dashboards with per-route token cost, model utilization, KV cache hit rate, and error counts.
6) Canary rollout: 10% traffic for 48 hours, 50% for 72 hours, evaluate regressions, then 100% cutover during low-traffic window.
7) Post-cutover audit: check cost deltas, fidelity regression alerts, and customer-facing latency SLAs.

Telemetries and KPIs to include in proposals
- Per-route 50/95/99 latency (ms)
- Token usage (input/output) per route and customer
- Per-token cost breakdown (serving runtime, caching, networking)
- KV cache hit rate and effective token reduction
- Model variant fallback rate and frequency of quantization-induced regressions
- GPU utilization, queue lengths, and batch sizes

Pricing and packaging guidance (sales-friendly language)
- For bursty/experimental customers: recommend hosted with volume discounts at 3 Tiers (0–10M tokens/mo, 10–100M, 100M+). Emphasize no-commit low-friction onboarding.
- For sustained high-throughput customers: recommend Dedicated with 6/12/24 month commits and an enterprise discount ladder; include an option for burst capacity at a premium.
- For regulated/air-gapped: price Private as a professional engagement plus platform fee and optional managed support. Include a setup/migration milestone schedule in the quote.

Example route configuration snippet (for Dedicated with batching and cache)
- JSON example (for sales/solutions engineers to show to customers):

{
  "route_name": "support-chat-v1",
  "deployment_mode": "dedicated",
  "model_pin": "redwood-medium-2/q4f16",
  "max_batch_size": "32",
  "max_wait_ms": "25",
  "kv_cache": "enabled",
  "fallbacks": ["redwood-medium-1/q4_int", "redwood-small-1/q4_int"]
}

Appendix: capacity-sim quick math (worked example)
Use this for a 24/7 customer with expected 150 QPS and average total tokens per request of 120 (input+output). Assume model throughput per GPU for the chosen variant is 4,000 tokens/sec at target latency band when batch_size=32.
- Expected tokens/sec = 150 QPS * 120 tokens = 18,000 tokens/sec.
- GPUs required (raw) = ceil(18,000 / 4,000) = 5 GPUs.
- Add buffer (autoscale / headroom) 25% -> 6 GPUs committed.
- Monthly amortized infra (example): 6 GPUs * $1,500/month = $9,000/month + storage/networking = $1,200/month -> $10,200/month platform fee amortized.
- Add per-token runtime costs and margin to build final price.

Benchmark checklist (three-day)
1) Collect traffic sample and sanitize PII.
2) Create replay harness with 5% variance to mimic burstiness.
3) Run at 0.5x, 1.0x, 1.25x expected peak.
4) Record 50/95/99 latencies, GPU traces, and fallback counts.
5) Run automated fidelity regression tests with a fixed prompt set; target no more than 2% regression on key metrics.
